transcript.text: Bosch induction hob PUE611BB1E making a loud buzzing/humming noise when I put my big stockpot on high. Is it about to break?

It is unlikely that your Bosch PUE611BB1E induction hob is "about to break" in the sense of imminent catastrophic failure, but the noise you are describing is a common phenomenon known as coil whine or electromagnetic humming. However, it can indicate an issue with compatibility or heat management.

Here’s a breakdown of what’s likely happening and what you should do:

### Why Induction Hobs Make Noise
Induction hobs work by creating a high-frequency electromagnetic field that induces currents in the ferrous (magnetic) base of your cookware. This causes the pot to heat up. The noise you hear is usually caused by:
1.  Vibration of the coil: The copper coils inside the hob vibrate at high frequencies due to the magnetic field.
2.  Resonance in the cookware: If the pot’s base isn’t perfectly flat or has a different thickness, it can resonate with the electromagnetic field, creating a buzzing or humming sound.

### Why It Happens Specifically with a "Big Stockpot" on High
• High Power Demand: On high settings, the hob draws maximum current and generates the strongest magnetic field, amplifying any vibration.
• Pot Compatibility/Quality: Not all induction-compatible pots are created equal. Some have thinner bases, uneven bottoms, or non-uniform magnetic properties that cause more resonance. Large stockpots often have larger surface areas that can act like a speaker diaphragm, amplifying the hum.
• Airflow/Cooling Fan: The hob has internal fans to cool the electronics. Under high load, these fans run faster and may produce a whining or buzzing noise that can be confused with coil whine.

### Is It Dangerous?
• Usually No: Occasional humming, especially with certain pots on high power, is normal for induction hobs.
• Watch for These Red Flags (Signs of Trouble):
• The noise is accompanied by a burning smell.
• The hob shuts off unexpectedly or displays an error code.
• The noise is extremely loud (like a jet engine) and persists even with different pots.
• You see visible sparks or the glass surface becomes excessively hot in spots unrelated to the pot.

### What You Can Do
1.  Test with Different Pots: Try using a smaller, high-quality induction-compatible pot on high power. If it’s quiet, the issue is likely cookware-related, not a hob fault.
2.  Check Pot Compatibility: Ensure your stockpot is explicitly labeled as "induction compatible" and has a flat, thick base. You can test this with a magnet—if it doesn’t stick firmly to the base, it may cause issues.
3.  Reduce Power Slightly: If the noise is only on the highest setting (e.g., level 9 or 10), try using level 8 or 7 for large pots. It may heat just as effectively with less noise.
4.  Ensure Proper Ventilation: Make sure there’s adequate space around the hob for airflow, especially if it’s built into a cabinet. Overheating can cause fans to work harder and make more noise.
5.  Clean the Hob Surface: Sometimes debris under or around the pot can exacerbate vibration. Ensure the bottom of the pot and the hob surface are clean and dry.

### When to Contact Bosch Support
If:
• The noise is new and significantly louder than before.
• It happens with all pots, not just one specific stockpot.
• You notice any error codes or performance issues (e.g., uneven heating).

Conclusion:
Your hob is likely functioning normally, but the combination of a large stockpot on high power is triggering electromagnetic resonance. Test with another pot first. If the noise persists across multiple compatible pots, contact Bosch customer support for advice, as it could indicate a failing component (like a capacitor or fan), though this is less common.

Note: Always refer to your user manual for specific troubleshooting steps and warranty information.

Thanks, that's helpful. I tried a few things: it only happens with the new stockpot and a cheap frying pan, my heavy cast iron pot is quiet. It's also much quieter at level 6 and below. No error codes and no burning smell. Does that point to the pans rather than the hob?

That strongly points to the pans being the culprit, not the hob itself. In fact, this is a very reassuring sign for your Bosch PUE611BB1E.

Here’s why your observations confirm it:

### 1. The "Cast Iron vs. Cheap Pan" Test
This is the most important clue. Induction hobs require cookware with a ferrous (magnetic) base to work. However, not all magnetic bases are created equal in terms of how they interact with the electromagnetic field.
• Heavy Cast Iron: These pots typically have thick, flat, and uniformly distributed magnetic bases. This allows for efficient energy transfer with minimal vibration or resonance. They also act as a massive heat sink, dampening any high-frequency vibrations from the coil.
• Cheap/New Stockpot & Frying Pan: Lower-quality or thinner-gauge pans often have:
• Uneven Bases: Even a slight warp can cause the pan to "chatter" against the magnetic field.
• Non-Uniform Magnetic Properties: The induction layer might be inconsistent, causing localized hot spots and vibrations.
• Thin Material: Thin metal vibrates more easily (like a drumhead), amplifying the high-frequency hum from the hob's coils into an audible buzz.

### 2. Noise Decreases at Lower Power Levels
Induction hobs generate noise primarily through:
• Coil Vibration: The higher the power, the stronger the magnetic field and the greater the vibration of the internal copper coils. At level 6 and below, the field is weaker, so less vibration occurs.
• Cooling Fan Noise: The hob’s internal fans run faster at high power to dissipate heat from the electronics. A louder fan can contribute to a "humming" sound that seems to come from the pan but is actually coming from under it.

### 3. No Error Codes or Burning Smell
This confirms the hob’s safety systems are functioning correctly and there is no electrical fault, overheating, or component failure.

### What You Can Do:
1.  Accept It as Normal: If the noise only happens with specific pans on high power, it’s a characteristic of those pans interacting with the induction field. Many induction hob owners experience this with certain cookware.
2.  Use Lower Power for Simmering: Since it’s quieter at level 6 and below, you can often achieve the same cooking result by starting on high to bring water to a boil, then reducing to level 4-5 for simmering. This will significantly reduce noise.
3.  Check Pan Compatibility: Ensure your new stockpot and cheap frying pan are explicitly labeled as "induction compatible." Look for the induction symbol (a coil) on the bottom. If they are old or very thin, they may simply be poor candidates for induction cooking.
4.  Ensure Flat Contact: Make sure the pans sit flat on the hob. Even a slight tilt can increase noise.

### When to Worry:
You should only contact Bosch support if:
• The noise starts happening with all your pots, including the quiet cast iron one.
• The noise becomes significantly louder over time, even at lower power levels.
• You notice any performance issues (e.g., hob not heating evenly, shutting off randomly).

In summary, your hob is likely fine. The noise is a combination of coil vibration and pan resonance, exacerbated by the specific characteristics of the cheaper/thinner pans you’re using on high power. Stick to your cast iron for quiet operation, or use lower power settings with the other pots.
